## Purpose

Fixes the consumer half of ROCm/mori#655 and the hang in #59114.

**The #59114 hang is only fixed when `write_recv_timeout` is set below the
client timeout.** With the 540s default and that report's ~400s client, the
client gives up first; at the deadline decode logs the timeout and the
scheduler ignores it for the already-aborted request.

In MoRIIO WRITE mode the consumer parks a request in `WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS`
until the producer's `write_done` arrives. If the producer dies that never
happens: the request waits until the client gives up, nothing is logged, and
`/health` stays 200. This adds a per-request receive timer on the consumer
scheduler; at the deadline the request is failed instead of wedging. It
complements ROCm/mori#670 (merged), which fails the producer-side transfer on a
QP error but still tells decode nothing.

Config: `kv_connector_extra_config["write_recv_timeout"]` (seconds, default 540,
finite and > 0, validated at startup). Documented in
`docs/features/moriio_connector_usage.md`.

Not a duplicate: the other open MoRIIO timeout PRs cover the prefill side
(#51301, #56465) or the handshake (#63856).

## Scope: this fails the request, it does not free the blocks

RDMA writes are one-sided, so a passed deadline does not prove the producer's NIC
has stopped; releasing a block could let a late write corrupt another request.
Blocks stay held until a real `finished_recving` (lifecycle split in #59382).
That `finished_recving` only reaches the scheduler with #59058, which keeps the
transfer mapping for a request that finishes mid-receive. So the second symptom
in #59114, KV usage staying elevated, is deliberately **not** fixed here.

## Design

* Armed in `update_state_after_alloc` on **every** consumer scheduler holding the
request (a DP rank that does not notify still waits for `write_done`).
* Stops on `finished_recving`, **not** when the request finishes: a request that
has its KV is never failed while it decodes.
* At the deadline the request id goes scheduler -> worker in
`MoRIIOConnectorMetadata.write_recv_timed_out_req_ids`, and every worker reports
it in `failed_recving` but **not** `finished_recving`. With
`kv_load_failure_policy="fail"` the scheduler fails the request and holds its
blocks (delayed free) until a real `finished_recving`.
* A client abort keeps the timer running (#59114); at the deadline the scheduler
ignores the failure for the already-aborted request, so it is not failed a
second time.
* Other connectors are unchanged. On `main`, `KVOutputAggregator` forwards a
failure only together with a finish, so at TP>1 a failed-only report would be
dropped. A new `KVConnectorBase_V1.reports_failed_recving_before_finished()`
(default `False`) lets a connector opt in to forwarding a receive that every
worker reported failed. Only MoRIIO in WRITE mode returns `True`;
`MultiConnector` returns `True` only if a child does. With `False` the
aggregator takes the same code path as on `main`.
* Works at any TP size and does not depend on the model: reporting by request id
through `failed_recving` is the path the scheduler requires for several KV cache
groups, and the delayed free is per request. So it covers every model MoRIIO
WRITE supports, including the attention + Mamba/KDA hybrids of #60544.
* The deadline starts at block allocation. Set it above worst-case prefill
queueing plus transfer time and below the client timeout. The 540s default
matches Mooncake's decode-side timeout (`VLLM_MOONCAKE_ABORT_REQUEST_TIMEOUT` +
60) and is under the OpenAI client's 600s default.
* Under `kv_load_failure_policy="recompute"` the timer is not armed, with a
startup warning: a failed receive cannot leave `WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS` there.
* A producer `write_failed` (#57705) stops the timer like any completed receive.

## Test plan

### Unit tests

`tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_moriio_write_recv_timeout.py` (`cpu_test`, no
GPU, RDMA or `mori` needed) runs the **real `Scheduler`**, the real
`KVOutputAggregator` (built via `from_connector`, as the executors do) and the
real `MoRIIOConnectorWorker.start_load_kv` / `get_transfer_results`, at TP=1 and
TP=2:

* producer dies: the request fails and its blocks stay allocated;
* producer is slow: the request fails with its blocks allocated, and the late
`write_done` then frees them.

The test injects the late `write_done` as a request id, so it checks the
scheduler side of the release; end to end that needs #59058.

`test_output_aggregator.py` covers both settings of the opt-in: without it, a
failed-only report waits for the finish as on `main`; with it, a failure from
every worker is forwarded.

+"""MoRIIO WRITE-mode consumer receive timeout (``write_recv_timeout``).

+``start_load_kv`` / ``get_transfer_results``, with no GPU or RDMA.

+TIMEOUT_S = 60.0

+
+class _Clock:
+    def __init__(self):
+        self.now = time.monotonic()
+
+    def monotonic(self) -> float:
+        return self.now
+
+    def __getattr__(self, name):
+        return getattr(time, name)
+
+
+def _make_consumer_worker() -> MoRIIOConnectorWorker:
+    worker = MoRIIOConnectorWorker.__new__(MoRIIOConnectorWorker)
+    worker.is_producer = False
+    worker.mode = MoRIIOMode.WRITE
+    worker.moriio_wrapper = SimpleNamespace(pop_failed_write_req_ids=list)
+    worker._unmatched_write_failures = OrderedDict()
+    worker._write_recv_timed_out = set()
+    worker.write_done = set()
+
+    def get_finished():
+        done, worker.write_done = worker.write_done, set()
+        return set(), done
+
+    worker.get_finished = get_finished  # type: ignore[method-assign]
+    return worker
+
+
+class _Engine:
+    """A decode instance: the real scheduler and one stub worker per TP rank."""
+
+    def __init__(self, monkeypatch, tp_size: int):
+        self.clock = _Clock()
+        monkeypatch.setattr(moriio_connector, "time", self.clock)
+        config = create_moriio_config(role="kv_consumer")
+        config.kv_transfer_config.kv_connector_extra_config["write_recv_timeout"] = (
+            TIMEOUT_S
+        )
+        self.scheduler = create_scheduler(config)
+        connector = self.scheduler.connector.connector_scheduler
+        monkeypatch.setattr(connector, "send_notify_block", lambda **kwargs: None)

+        self.workers = [_make_consumer_worker() for _ in range(tp_size)]
+        # Like the executors: only multi-worker outputs are aggregated.
+        self.aggregator = (
+            KVOutputAggregator.from_connector(self.scheduler.connector, tp_size)
+            if tp_size > 1
+            else None
+        )
+
+    def step(self, write_done: frozenset[str] = frozenset()):
+        self.finish(self.scheduler.schedule(), write_done)
+
+    def finish(self, out, write_done: frozenset[str] = frozenset()):
+        scheduled = [self.scheduler.requests[i] for i in out.num_scheduled_tokens]
+        outputs = []
+        for worker in self.workers:
+            worker.start_load_kv(out.kv_connector_metadata)
+            worker.write_done |= write_done
+            results = worker.get_transfer_results()
+            output = create_model_runner_output(
+                scheduled, finished_recving=results.finished_recving
+            )
+            output.kv_connector_output.failed_recving = results.failed_recving
+            outputs.append(output)
+        if self.aggregator is not None:
+            outputs = [self.aggregator.aggregate(outputs)]
+        self.scheduler.update_from_output(out, outputs[0])
+
+    def add_waiting_request(self):
+        request = create_request(
+            num_tokens=4 * self.scheduler.block_size, do_remote_prefill=True
+        )
+        _setup_kv_transfer_request(request)
+        self.scheduler.add_request(request)
+        self.step()
+        assert request.status == RequestStatus.WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS
+        return request
+
+
+@pytest.fixture(params=[1, 2], ids=["tp1", "tp2"])
+def engine(request, monkeypatch):
+    role = moriio_common.get_role()
+    moriio_common.set_role(moriio_common.ROLE.CONSUMER)
+    yield _Engine(monkeypatch, request.param)
+    moriio_common.set_role(role)
+

+def test_prefill_dies_request_fails_and_blocks_stay_allocated(engine):
+    free_before = engine.pool.get_num_free_blocks()
+    request = engine.add_waiting_request()
+    held = engine.pool.get_num_free_blocks()
+    assert held < free_before
+
+    engine.clock.now += TIMEOUT_S - 1
+    engine.step()
+    assert request.status == RequestStatus.WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS
+
+    engine.clock.now += 2
+    engine.step()
+    assert request.status == RequestStatus.FINISHED_ERROR
+    engine.clock.now += 10 * TIMEOUT_S
+    for _ in range(3):
+        engine.step()
+    assert request.request_id in engine.scheduler.requests
+    assert engine.pool.get_num_free_blocks() == held
+
+
+def test_prefill_slow_request_fails_and_blocks_freed_on_late_write_done(engine):
+    free_before = engine.pool.get_num_free_blocks()
+    request = engine.add_waiting_request()
+    held = engine.pool.get_num_free_blocks()
+
+    engine.clock.now += TIMEOUT_S + 1
+    engine.step()
+    assert request.status == RequestStatus.FINISHED_ERROR
+    assert engine.pool.get_num_free_blocks() == held
+
+    engine.step(write_done=frozenset({request.request_id}))
+    assert request.request_id not in engine.scheduler.requests
+    assert engine.pool.get_num_free_blocks() == free_before
+
+
+def test_timeout_reported_once_when_two_schedules_precede_the_output(engine):
+    """Batch queue / async scheduling: step N+1 is scheduled before the output
+    of step N is processed."""
+    request = engine.add_waiting_request()
+    held = engine.pool.get_num_free_blocks()
+    engine.clock.now += TIMEOUT_S + 1
+
+    first = engine.scheduler.schedule()
+    second = engine.scheduler.schedule()
+    assert first.kv_connector_metadata.write_recv_timed_out_req_ids == {
+        request.request_id
+    }
+    assert not second.kv_connector_metadata.write_recv_timed_out_req_ids
+
+    engine.finish(first)
+    engine.finish(second)
+    assert request.status == RequestStatus.FINISHED_ERROR
+    assert engine.pool.get_num_free_blocks() == held

I wonder if the watchdog might be better cleared when the receive finishes rather than when the request finishes. I think the two can diverge in a couple of ways:

Too early: a client abort while waiting disarms it, but the scheduler keeps the blocks until finished_recving arrives. That's the #59114 case; details in my comment there (link).

@ErliCai thanks — you were right on both counts, and both are fixed in the
revision I just pushed. I also reproduced each divergence on hardware first so
the change isn't just reasoning.

**Too early.** Confirmed, and it is exactly #59114. With a client timeout below
the deadline, `request_finished` disarmed the timer before it could fire: the
watchdog never ran and consumer KV stayed elevated for the rest of the
observation with no traffic. The timer is now kept across an abort — the request
is marked orphaned and still timed, since the scheduler holds its blocks
regardless of what the client did. At the deadline an orphaned request gets a
log line rather than a second terminal outcome.

**Too late.** Also confirmed as a real hazard: `_handle_invalid_blocks` scans
`self.running` with `evict_blocks=True`, so a request that had already received
its KV and was still decoding would have been failed. The timer is now stopped
on *receive* completion in `update_connector_output`, which is the change you
proposed. I instrumented a build to log every arm and every `finished_recving`:
the counts match exactly, the ids are identical, and a successful request now
sits well past its deadline untouched.

Two things beyond your comment, since they change the shape of the PR:

**It no longer reclaims.** Per the lifecycle split in #59382, a timeout now
fails the request but does not free its blocks — a one-sided RDMA write can
still land, so releasing could corrupt a block that has been handed to another
request. Blocks stay held until a real `finished_recving`. The title and the log
line changed accordingly; the old "Reclaiming N block(s)" message was claiming
something that never happened. This does mean the KV-usage half of #59114 is
deliberately not fixed here — that needs #59058 plus a no-further-writes
guarantee that MoRI-IO does not currently expose at per-request granularity.

**Own blocks only.** `get_block_ids()` also returns prefix-cache hits shared
with other requests, so reporting them at the deadline would have failed those
requests too; NIXL and Mooncake use the unhashed ids for the same reason. Tested
with the cache actually warm: a request whose prefix was ~99.6% cached reported
**1 block** rather than the 256 it referenced.

The rebase onto current main also turned up something worth flagging to you and
@YukioZzz: #51052 added a `get_block_ids_with_load_errors` to
`MoRIIOConnectorWorker` after this PR was opened, and this PR had added one of
its own. Both definitions merge cleanly and Python keeps the later one, so the
timeout drain was silently shadowed — green rebase, dead feature, no error. I
removed this PR's copy and routed timed-out blocks through the existing
`_invalid_block_ids` set, so the two paths now share one drain. Worth knowing
that method is doing double duty for READ load failures and WRITE timeouts.

Validation is in the PR description. Happy to adjust the lifecycle split if you
or @yuzhouo7 read #59382 differently.

+"""WRITE-mode consumer receive timeout of the MoRIIO connector.
+
+In WRITE mode the decode side parks a request in ``WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS``
+until the producer's ``write_done`` arrives. If the producer dies that never
+happens, so the scheduler arms a per-request timer, configured by
+``kv_connector_extra_config["write_recv_timeout"]`` (seconds, default 540).
+These tests pin the configuration and the lifecycle:
+
+  * the timeout is read from ``kv_connector_extra_config``, validated at
+    startup;
+  * the timer is armed with the request's *own* (unhashed) blocks only, so a
+    prefix-cache hit shared with another request is never reported;
+  * a timeout fails a live request but never frees its blocks -- RDMA writes
+    are one-sided, so a late write can still land (vllm-project/vllm#59382);
+  * a client abort keeps the timer running, and at the deadline the request is
+    logged as orphaned instead of failed a second time (#59114);
+  * the timer stops when the receive completes, not when the request finishes,
+    so a request that already has its KV is never failed while it decodes.
+
+They run on the scheduler alone, with no GPU and no RDMA.
+"""
+

@@ -133,6 +133,8 @@ WRITE mode is used by default. READ mode can be configured by setting `--kv-tran
     - WRITE mode: **Block allocation:** the decoder notifies the prefiller about its block ids, so the prefiller can push its computed KV blocks into the correct place on the decoder instance. **Completion:** once all blocks have been transferred, the prefiller notifies the decoder that it's safe to use its blocks.
     - READ mode: **Completion:** once the decoder has read all blocks from the prefiller, it notifies the prefiller so it can free its KV cache blocks.
 
+- `write_recv_timeout`: WRITE mode, decoder only. Seconds (default `540`, must be finite and greater than zero) the decoder waits for the prefiller's completion notification before failing the request. This keeps a request from hanging forever in `WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS` when the prefiller dies or its notification is lost. The timer starts when the decoder allocates the request's blocks, so set it above your worst-case prefill queueing plus transfer time, and below your client timeout so the decoder acts first. A timed-out request is failed but its KV blocks are **not** freed, because a late one-sided RDMA write could still land in them. They stay allocated until the decoder restarts; releasing them when a late completion arrives is tracked in [#59058](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59058). It only takes effect with the default `kv_load_failure_policy` of `fail`.

+"""WRITE-mode consumer receive timeout of the MoRIIO connector.
+
+In WRITE mode the decode side parks a request in ``WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS``
+until the producer's ``write_done`` arrives. If the producer dies that never
+happens, so the scheduler arms a per-request timer, configured by
+``kv_connector_extra_config["write_recv_timeout"]`` (seconds, default 540).
+These tests pin the configuration and the lifecycle:
+
+  * the timeout is read from ``kv_connector_extra_config``, validated at
+    startup;
+  * the timer is armed with the request's *own* (unhashed) blocks only, so a
+    prefix-cache hit shared with another request is never reported;
+  * a timeout fails a live request but never frees its blocks -- RDMA writes
+    are one-sided, so a late write can still land (vllm-project/vllm#59382);
+  * a client abort keeps the timer running, and at the deadline the request is
+    logged as orphaned instead of failed a second time (#59114);
+  * the timer stops when the receive completes, not when the request finishes,
+    so a request that already has its KV is never failed while it decodes.
+
+They run on the scheduler alone, with no GPU and no RDMA.
+"""

+import math

+from unittest.mock import MagicMock

+pytestmark = [pytest.mark.cpu_test, pytest.mark.skip_global_cleanup]

+def _make_scheduler(timeout: float = TIMEOUT_S) -> MoRIIOConnectorScheduler:
+    """A WRITE-mode consumer scheduler without the heavy real ``__init__``."""
+    scheduler = MoRIIOConnectorScheduler.__new__(MoRIIOConnectorScheduler)
+    scheduler.is_producer = False
+    scheduler.mode = MoRIIOMode.WRITE
+    scheduler.tp_size = 1

+    scheduler._global_dp_rank = 0

+    scheduler._reqs_need_pending_save = {}

+    scheduler._write_recv_block_ids = {}

+def _make_blocks(
+    own_ids: list[int], shared_ids: list[int] | None = None
+) -> KVCacheBlocks:
+    """Allocation of one KV cache group.
+
+    ``shared_ids`` are prefix-cache hits: full blocks that carry a hash and are
+    referenced by other requests too. ``own_ids`` are the request's own
+    unhashed blocks.
+    """
+    shared = [KVCacheBlock(block_id=i) for i in shared_ids or []]
+    for block in shared:
+        block.set_block_hash(
+            make_block_hash_with_group_id(BlockHash(b"hash-%d" % block.block_id), 0)
+        )
+    own = [KVCacheBlock(block_id=i) for i in own_ids]
+    return KVCacheBlocks(blocks=(shared + own,))
+
+
+def _make_request(request_id: str = REQ_ID):
+    # A plain request id carries no router-embedded ZMQ address, so the notify
+    # target comes from kv_transfer_params, as with the routing sidecar.
+    return SimpleNamespace(
+        request_id=request_id,
+        status=RequestStatus.WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS,
+        kv_transfer_params={
+            "do_remote_prefill": True,
+            "do_remote_decode": False,
+            "transfer_id": f"xfer-{request_id}",
+            "remote_host": "127.0.0.1",
+            "remote_notify_port": 7000,
+        },
+    )
+
+
+def _arm(
+    scheduler: MoRIIOConnectorScheduler,
+    request=None,
+    blocks: KVCacheBlocks | None = None,
+    num_external_tokens: int = 32,
+):
+    request = request or _make_request()
+    blocks = blocks or _make_blocks(own_ids=[10, 11])
+    scheduler.update_state_after_alloc(request, blocks, num_external_tokens)
+    return request
+
+
+def _abort(scheduler: MoRIIOConnectorScheduler, request):
+    """The client gave up while the request was still waiting for its KV."""
+    request.status = RequestStatus.FINISHED_ABORTED
+    return scheduler.request_finished(request, block_ids=[[10, 11]])
+
+
+def _expire(scheduler: MoRIIOConnectorScheduler, request_id: str = REQ_ID):
+    """Move a request's deadline into the past instead of sleeping."""
+    scheduler._write_recv_deadline[request_id] = time.monotonic() - 1.0

+    )

+            kv_connector_extra_config={
+                "read_mode": False,
+                "host_ip": "127.0.0.1",
+                "handshake_port": 6001,
+                "notify_port": 6002,
+                **(extra_config or {}),
+            },
+            kv_role="kv_consumer",
+            kv_load_failure_policy=kv_load_failure_policy,
+        ),
+        speculative_config=None,
+        cache_config=SimpleNamespace(block_size=16, mamba_cache_mode="all"),
+        scheduler_config=SimpleNamespace(disable_hybrid_kv_cache_manager=True),
+        num_lookahead_tokens=0,

+        parallel_config=SimpleNamespace(

+            decode_context_parallel_size=1,
+            data_parallel_rank=0,
+            data_parallel_size_local=1,
+            data_parallel_size=1,
+        ),

+def test_default_timeout_is_the_documented_constant():

This removed the block-id tracking, the single-group guard (so it also works for hybrid / multi-group now) and the orphan bookkeeping: an aborted request is already finished, so the scheduler simply ignores its failure.

One finding while doing this. With TP > 1, KVOutputAggregator only emitted failed_recving together with finished_recving (failed = pending & finished), so a failed-only report was silently dropped; with TP = 1 there is no aggregation, so it went straight through. I changed the aggregator to also forward a receive that every worker reported failed, counting failures the same way it counts finishes (so outputs replayed from failed workers still count). Connectors that follow the existing contract (failed implies finished on the same rank) see no change. I documented the failed-only case in KVConnectorTransferResults. Happy to split this core change into its own PR if you prefer.

Suggestion 2 (tests). Trimmed to your two scenarios, through the real Scheduler and the real worker start_load_kv / get_transfer_results, at TP = 1 and TP = 2 (TP = 2 goes through the aggregator):

P dies: D times out, the request is failed, its blocks stay allocated.
P is slow: D times out, the request is failed with its blocks still allocated, and the late write_done then frees them.

One caveat on scenario 2. The test hands the worker the late write_done already translated to the request id. In the real path that translation fails today: when the request fails, request_finished drops the consumer's transfer_id -> request_id mapping, so a late write_done stays unmatched and the blocks are held until restart. #59058 keeps that mapping for a request that finishes mid-receive, so the test checks the scheduler side of the release and #59058 provides the delivery. I kept the two separate to avoid conflicting with it.
Suggestion 3 (comments). Removed most of them.

Follow-up (safe reclaim). Agreed that freeing after a timeout alone is unsafe. One nuance on the Z.AI approach as I read their post: D frees only after P positively replies that it is safe to reclaim (no writes started, or all completed). The case that stays hard is a P that is dead or unreachable, because "no reply" doesn't prove its NIC has stopped writing. We're prototyping a receiver-side fence in MoRI for that (ROCm/mori#848): D revokes P's remote access to the request's memory first, then frees, which is safe whether P is slow or dead. I'll follow up separately once it's validated.
The description still describes the block-id version.

Thanks @okorzh-amd, updated for c26917d: timeouts are reported by request id in `failed_recving` (not `finished_recving`), the aggregator rule is opt-in so other connectors are unchanged, and the test plan and hardware run reflect the current code.

Thanks @simondanielsson, all your comments are addressed in c26917d, and @okorzh-amd the description is updated.

The main change is to the aggregator: its new rule is now opt-in through a connector hook that defaults to off, and only MoRIIO WRITE turns it on. Other connectors run the same code as on `main`, and the timeout works at any TP size.

I think the problem we're trying to solve makes sense, but I think we can simplify this a bit. **Suggestion 1**: Can we please see if we can refactor this to instead use the `failed_recving` hook rather than the invalid_block_ids hook? Since the latter explicitly doesn't support hybrid/swa models we will eventually need another similar fix for those models. I think we might be able to just add the timed out request to failed_recving but **not** simulatenously add it to done_recving. Can you check if this would make things simpler? Reminder: finished_recving means the request can be either (a) scheduled in the next step or (b) freed. Failed_recving means the scheduler will fail the request **Suggestion 2**: Let's trim the test suite and just keep one or two that encapsulates this bug and the intended behavior. I.e. 1. P dies: send a request, kill the P instance, the D eventually times out, the requests is aborted/failed, but **blocks remain allocated**. (the allocation part needs a separate fix, but that's for a different PR, as you correctly say) 2. P is just slow: send a request, assume the d instance triggers its timeout, the request is failed but blocks are still allocated on D, P eventually writes into the blocks and send write_done, then the blocks are correctly freed. IMO this maps quite well to my understanding of the bug (to re-iterate) > **Setup**: In WRITE mode, decode allocates blocks and sends a message to prefill saying "write here", and then parks the request in WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVs. The request is only scheduled after recving a `write_done` from prefill > **Problem:** two cases > 1. if prefill dies, it never sends this `write_done` message to decode. Decode hence holds the blocks indefinitely > 2. if prefill is extremely slow (unbounded?), the decode might be stuck forever waiting for the write_done message. **One solution that doesn't work**: You already saidd this but just to re-iterate: add a timeout on decode and _free the blocks after the timeout_. This does't work because if the prefill simply takes longer than this timeout, the write will override the recycled blocks (see [this Z.AI blogpost if you're interested](https://z.ai/blog/scaling-pain)!) ** **Suggestion 3**: Let's remove most of the comments. Save them for explaining parts of the code that really needs an explanation 👍 **As a followup:** to fix the issue with indefinite allocations on D if P dies, I think we need to a mechanism for D to ask P if it's safe to reclaim the blocks. This is exactly what ZAI did in the above mentioned blogpost. I.e. D sends `request_aborted` to P, and if P is live then it responds with `dont_free_blocks`, and D then doesn't free its blocks. In contrast, if P is dead, then D will never get the `dont_free_blocks` reply, and hence it can go ahead and free the blocks.
Thanks for the fixes, it looks much better now!
